comparison: Perfect alignment on claims C1, C2, C14-C20 regarding prior work on value-RNN learning and biological implausibility of BPTT. Both evaluations find these background claims well-supported by appropriate citations and established knowledge.

Perfect alignment on claims C71-C78 regarding probabilistic reward schedule experiments. Both evaluations accept that models successfully replicate experimental findings with TD-RPE patterns shown in Figures 4F-H.
Perfect alignment on claims C98-C100 regarding probabilistic task results with biological constraints. Both evaluations accept that constraints preserve learning capability as shown in Figures 7A-D.

Perfect alignment on claims C111-C114 regarding E-I unit results and mathematical equivalence. Both evaluations accept the empirical results in Figures 9B-C and the mathematical justification without challenge.
Perfect alignment on claims C115-C118 regarding distractor experiments. Both evaluations accept the robustness results in Figure 10 as important validation for ecological validity.
Perfect alignment on claims C119-C123 regarding action selection tasks. Both evaluations accept that the approach extends beyond pure value learning, with results shown in Figure 11.

Perfect alignment on claims C21-C29 regarding feedback alignment literature and gap identification. Both evaluations accept the novelty of extending feedback alignment to TD learning and find the motivation well-articulated.

Perfect alignment on claims C124-C129 regarding predictions and implications. Both evaluations accept these as logical extensions appropriately framed as testable predictions, though some are more directly testable than others.
Perfect alignment on claims C8-C13 regarding neuroscientific background on dopamine and TD learning. Both evaluations accept these well-established findings from literature without challenge.

Strong alignment on claims C6-C7, C31, C85-C91 regarding non-negative constraints. Both evaluations find this a key contribution with extensive experimental support in Figures 6 and 8. Peer reviewer 3 explicitly highlights non-negative FA as the most valuable theoretical insight. OpenEval R8 covers C6-C7, C31, C85-C91 while Peer R3 additionally includes C101-C104, C107 on loose alignment mechanisms.

Substantial overlap on main findings (C3, C30, C51) that random feedback works for TD learning. OpenEval R2 covers C3-C5, C30, C51 focusing on mechanistic explanation, while Peer R1 covers broader experimental results C3, C30, C47-C56, C59-C60. Both find claims well-supported by systematic simulations and statistical tests.

Strong overlap on experimental results claims C47-C49, C52-C56. OpenEval R3 focuses on systematic experimental methodology with statistical tests in Figure 2, while Peer R1 encompasses these within broader acceptance of the main demonstration including C3, C30, C59-C60.

Strong alignment on feedback alignment mechanism claims C61-C63. OpenEval R5 covers C61-C63 on alignment and correlation with performance, while Peer R2 covers C61-C63, C68-C69 on alignment dynamics. Both accept the extension to TD learning with data from Figures 3A-E.

Alignment on feedback alignment dynamics claims C68-C69. OpenEval R6 focuses on mechanistic insight about online learning constraints, while Peer R2 includes these within broader acceptance of feedback alignment mechanism along with C61-C63.

Partial overlap on loose alignment mechanism claims C101-C104. OpenEval R11 focuses on geometric constraints and mechanistic explanation from Figure 8A, while Peer R3 includes these claims within broader evaluation of non-negative constraints (C6-C7, C31, C85-C91, C101-C104, C107).

Strong alignment on weight decay manipulation claims C109-C110. Both evaluations accept that decay manipulation provides mechanistic insight about alignment dynamics, with results in Figures 8E-G. OpenEval R13 also covers C108.

Partial overlap on PCA analysis claims C57-C58. OpenEval R4 covers detailed statistical analysis C57-C60 on PC contributions, while Peer R9 accepts C57-C58, C94 as mechanistic insight into representational structure without challenge.

Partial overlap on early trial advantage claims C95-C96. OpenEval R9 covers broader mechanistic findings C92-C97 including early trial dynamics, while Peer R10 specifically accepts C95-C96 as temporal dynamics insight from Figure 6I.

Alignment on mechanistic principles claims C4-C5. OpenEval R2 includes these within main findings evaluation (C3-C5, C30, C51), while Peer R14 separately evaluates C4-C5 as established theoretical foundation accepted by all reviewers.

Minimal overlap on claim C107 regarding correlation between initial alignment and performance. OpenEval R12 covers C105-C107 on temporal aspects of alignment, while Peer R3 includes C107 within broader non-negative constraints evaluation.

OpenEval R18 evaluates biological constraints claims C79-C84 (firing rates, projection types, plasticity) as well-supported by established knowledge and citations. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found, though these constraints are implicitly accepted throughout peer reviews.

OpenEval R21 evaluates model architecture and assumptions claims C32-C46 as clearly stated and justified. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found, though the model architecture is implicitly accepted by peer reviewers in their evaluation of results.

Minor overlap on claims C59-C60 regarding PC structure correlation with learning. OpenEval R4 focuses on detailed PC analysis C57-C60, while Peer R1 includes C59-C60 within broader experimental results acceptance.

Minimal overlap on claim C94 regarding PCA analysis. OpenEval R9 covers mechanistic findings C92-C97 including C94 on PC structure, while Peer R9 accepts C57-C58, C94 as uncontested mechanistic insight.
